awd_titl_txt: Ricci Flows and Steady Ricci Solitons
awd_abstract_narration:
This award supports research in differential geometry focusing on Ricci flows. These flows are defined on manifolds equipped with a metric, that is to say, a way of measuring distance. A Ricci flow is a geometric partial differential equation for Riemannian metrics. The Ricci flow tends to evolve an initial metric into a more homogeneous one. The singularity analysis of Ricci flow is a central subject, as it helps to understand the geometry and topology of manifolds. The most remarkable application in this direction is the resolution of the Poincare conjecture and the Geometrization conjecture by Perelman. Many of the Ricci flow singularity models are Ricci solitons. Recent examples of solitons constructed by the PI look like flying wings. The PI will study the geometry of all 3-dimensional steady Ricci solitons and try to classify them by their asymptotic limits. In addition, the PI will study the higher-dimensional steady Ricci solitons and see if they can arise as singularity models.



The research project is split into two projects. The first project is to prove the O(2)-symmetry of all 3-dimensional steady Ricci solitons. This includes showing that the Bryant soliton is the unique 3-dimensional steady Ricci soliton that is asymptotic to a ray. This extends a previous result of the PI in which one assumes the O(2)-symmetry of the soliton. The PI developed some methods that may be extended to the more general class of ancient collapsed Ricci flows in dimension 3. In particular, the PI will investigate the symmetry of the ancient collapsed Ricci flows in dimension 3 and aim at classifying them by certain 2-dimensional limits. The second project is a continuation of the PI's work on the existence theory of Ricci flows coming out of non-compact initial manifolds. The PI will investigate the applications of non-compact Ricci flows in topology and geometry.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This project advanced the mathematical study of curvature, geometric evolution equations, and the relationship between geometry and topology. Its primary focus was Ricci flow, an equation that changes the geometry of a space over time by smoothing variations in curvature. Ricci flow has become a central tool in differential geometry, with applications to the classification of geometric spaces and the analysis of singularities. The project also investigated Ricci solitons, special geometries that model the behavior of Ricci flow near singularities.

One outcome concerned the topology of complete, noncompact three-dimensional spaces with positive scalar curvature. In joint work with Otis Chodosh and Kai Xu, the project proved that a complete contractible three-manifold with positive scalar curvature and bounded geometry must be topologically equivalent to ordinary three-dimensional Euclidean space. The work also showed that open handlebodies with more than one handle cannot admit complete metrics satisfying these geometric conditions. These findings demonstrate that positive scalar curvature, when combined with appropriate geometric control, places strong restrictions on the possible global topology of a space. The proof introduced new applications of a weak form of inverse mean curvature flow, an evolution process in which surfaces expand according to their curvature. This work was published in Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics.

A second outcome addressed the formation of singularities under Ricci flow. In joint work with Kyeongsu Choi, the project established the long-time existence of a related evolution equation called harmonic map heat flow in settings where a Ricci flow approaches a compact shrinking model. This provides a consistent coordinate system, or “gauge,” for comparing the evolving geometry with its limiting model. The method eliminates ambiguity caused by changes of coordinates and leads to uniqueness results and quantitative estimates for the rate of convergence. As applications, the work constructed and classified ancient Ricci flows approaching compact integrable shrinking solitons and obtained optimal convergence rates for flows developing singularities modeled on these spaces.

A third outcome concerned steady Kähler–Ricci solitons, which combine Ricci-flow geometry with the additional structure of complex geometry. In joint work with Pak-Yeung Chan and Ronan J. Conlon, the project constructed new families of complete, positively curved solitons on complex Euclidean spaces of complex dimension at least three. These examples have less symmetry than previously known classical examples. Consequently, the work shows that even strong positivity of curvature does not force full rotational symmetry or uniqueness. The family connects previously known model geometries and provides a complex-geometric analogue of the “flying-wing” solitons arising in Riemannian geometry. 

The project’s intellectual merit lies in its new classification and rigidity theorems, new geometric examples, and new analytical methods for studying curvature and geometric flows. Its broader impacts include strengthening the publicly available foundation of mathematical knowledge and creating connections among geometric analysis, topology, complex geometry, and nonlinear partial differential equations. Results were disseminated through journal publication, freely accessible research manuscripts, seminars, and collaboration among researchers at multiple institutions.
